section_summary: This section documents proceedings and political debates of the Japanese Imperial Diet from February 1934 to January 1935, as reported by the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo and analyzed by the Department of State. It covers the regular 65th session and the November–December 1934 extraordinary session, highlighting conflicts over disproportionate military budgets versus rural disaster and agrarian relief, the decline of party power following the Okada Cabinet's confrontation with the Seiyukai, and political controversies such as the Ashikaga historical loyalty dispute. In addition, the section traces Japan's foreign policy pronouncements by Foreign Minister Koki Hirota, including Japan's notification to terminate the Washington Naval Treaty, diplomatic maneuvers toward China and the Soviet Union, and American and British assessments of Japanese intentions.

subfiles.about: A collection of Tokyo newspaper clippings reporting on parliamentary debates during the 65th session of the Diet, including discussions of naval policy, military reform, the May 15 incident trials, and the Takauji Ashikaga controversy.
subfiles.summary: This series of clippings from The Japan Advertiser (including translations of articles from Asahi and Kokumin) covers interpellations and ministerial replies in the Imperial Diet from February 4 to February 8, 1934. Navy Minister Mineo Osumi addresses naval disarmament policy, the London and Washington treaties, and controversy surrounding Vice-Admiral Nobumasa Suetsugu's comments about Charles Lindbergh. War Minister Senjuro Hayashi discusses army reorganization and defense needs, while interpellators criticize the disproportionate military budget relative to agricultural relief. The clippings also report on fierce attacks against Commerce Minister Kumakichi Nakajima for an article praising the historical figure Takauji Ashikaga, interpellations regarding Sino-Japanese and Soviet relations, and debate over the iron industry merger bill.
subfiles.title: Press Clippings on Japanese Diet Proceedings and Political Controversies

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet indexing an instruction sent to the American Embassy in Tokyo regarding legislative action on Japanese export subsidies.
subfiles.summary: This document file note cross-references telegram No. 30 sent to Japan on March 14, 1934, filed under decimal file 611.9417/17. The telegram instructed American diplomatic officers in Tokyo to report any Japanese legislative action relating to direct or indirect grants-in-aid provided by the Japanese Government to promote the export of Japanese goods.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 30 to Tokyo Regarding Japanese Export Subsidies

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet and attached extract from Tokyo Periodic Report No. 76 summarizing the accomplishments and legislative record of the 65th session of the Imperial Diet.
subfiles.summary: This document comprises a document file note (894.032/13) and attached extract from Ambassador Grew's political report for March 1934 (despatch dated April 16, 1934). It reviews the adjournment of the 65th Diet on March 26, 1934, highlighting the passage of the budget and forty-eight out of fifty submitted government bills, despite dissatisfaction over inadequate farm relief and corruption charges that led to the resignation of Education Minister Hatoyama. The extract includes an itemized list of forty-one bills passed without amendment, encompassing oil industry control, foreign trade adjustment, military service modifications, and disaster tax relief.
subfiles.title: Periodic Report Extract on Accomplishments of the 65th Session of the Diet

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet and attached table reporting the opening of the 65th Diet and the political party alignments in both houses of the parliament.
subfiles.summary: This document consists of a document file note referencing Tokyo Periodic Report No. 74 of February 6, 1934, along with an attached table detailing parliamentary party strengths following the opening of the Diet on January 23, 1934. The table enumerates membership in the House of Peers across groups such as the Kenkyukai, Koseikai, Dowakai, and Kayokai, totaling 396 members. In the House of Representatives, party standings are recorded as 291 for the Seiyukai, 120 for the Minseito, 32 for the Kokumin Domei, 8 for the First Lobby Group, and 15 vacancies, totaling 466 seats.
subfiles.title: Document File Note and Table on Diet Opening and Parliamentary Party Alignment

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet and attached extract from Tokyo Periodic Report No. 88 (Despatch No. 1007) discussing political agitation for an extraordinary session of the Diet following natural disasters.
subfiles.summary: This document includes a document file note and an attached extract from Ambassador Grew's political report for September 1934, dated October 11, 1934. It details demands by the Seiyukai and other political groups for a special Diet session to address farm relief for rice and silk cocoon producers. The Cabinet of Admiral Okada, which had resisted these demands, finally agreed on September 28 to convene a special session following the devastating Osaka typhoon and tidal wave of September 21, 1934, after an inspection tour by Home Minister Goto.
subfiles.title: Periodic Report Extract on Diet Proceedings and Demand for an Extraordinary Session

subfiles.about: A telegram from Ambassador Grew reporting that Japanese Foreign Minister Koki Hirota's address before the Diet has been telegraphed to the Japanese Embassy in Washington.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew informs the Secretary of State that Japanese Foreign Office spokesman Eiji Amau notified an embassy staff member that Foreign Minister Koki Hirota's address delivered to the Diet on the morning of November 30, 1934, was cabled in full to the Japanese Embassy in Washington for press distribution. Consequently, Grew states that he will not transmit a telegraphic summary of the address.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 264 from Tokyo Regarding Foreign Minister Hirota's Diet Speech

subfiles.about: A Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing the proceedings and political significance of the extraordinary session of the Japanese Diet reported in Tokyo Despatch No. 1088.
subfiles.summary: Written by William T. Turner in the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, this memorandum summarizes Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 1088 concerning the special session of the Japanese Diet convened on November 28, 1934. It highlights the enactment of relief measures, including two supplementary budgets totaling over 81 million yen, despite contentious interpellations on high military appropriations and deficit financing. Turner emphasizes the political outcomes: the defeat and loss of prestige of the Seiyukai, the setback to constitutional party government, and the continued political dominance of the military.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1088 Regarding Extraordinary Diet Proceedings

subfiles.about: A comprehensive diplomatic despatch reporting on the proceedings, political clashes, and legislative results of the extraordinary session of the Japanese Diet held in November and December 1934.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on the extraordinary Diet session convened from November 28 to December 10, 1934, called primarily to enact disaster and depression relief for distressed agrarian districts. While the government sought to limit debate to relief, interpellations challenged high military spending, deficit bond issues, Manchurian expenditures, and the Army's controversial political pamphlet. Grew analyzes major political developments, including the Okada Cabinet's successful showdown against the Seiyukai over an obstructionist 180-million-yen budget amendment, the declining influence of political parties, Finance Minister Takahashi's adroit parliamentary performance, and the passage of supplementary relief appropriations amounting to over 81 million yen.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1088: Proceedings of the Extraordinary Session of the Diet

subfiles.about: A brief telegram from Ambassador Grew notifying the Department that the text of Foreign Minister Hirota's annual address to the Diet is available at the Japanese Embassy in Washington.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew informs the Secretary of State that the text of the annual foreign policy address delivered on January 22, 1935, by Foreign Minister Koki Hirota before the Imperial Diet has been made available to the press and public through the Japanese Embassy in Washington.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 12 from Tokyo Regarding Availability of Foreign Minister Hirota's Speech Text

subfiles.about: A diplomatic despatch from the American Embassy in London transmitting British press reports and editorial comment on Japanese Foreign Minister Koki Hirota's annual address to the Diet.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires ad interim Ray Atherton reports on British press coverage of Foreign Minister Hirota's January 22, 1935 speech before the Japanese Diet, noting that while general commentary was limited, The Times of London gave it prominent attention. Atherton observes that diplomatic observers suspected Ambassador Matsudaira of having held confidential discussions with British officials regarding Far Eastern policy while conducting naval talks. Enclosures include articles and an editorial from The Times analyzing Japan's proclaimed role as the stabilizing power in East Asia, its policy toward China, Manchuria, and the Soviet Union, and its termination of the Washington Naval Treaty alongside hopes for a new disarmament formula.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1178: British Press Reporting on Japanese Foreign Minister's Annual Speech to the Diet

subfiles.about: A memorandum by Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, analyzing Japanese Foreign Minister Koki Hirota's annual foreign policy speech to the Diet.
subfiles.summary: Transmitting a copy of Foreign Minister Koki Hirota's January 22, 1935 address before the Diet, Stanley K. Hornbeck provides a detailed analysis for Secretary of State Cordell Hull. Hornbeck emphasizes that the speech was crafted primarily to shape international opinion while reaffirming Japan's established foreign policy. He breaks down the address into five aspects: the political significance of the upcoming visit of the Emperor of Manchukuo, naval limitation principles designed to sway British and American public opinion, relations with the United States, outwardly friendly overtures toward the Soviet Union coupled with demands to demilitarize frontiers, and relations with China. Hornbeck concludes that the address demonstrates no genuine policy shift and cautions the U.S. government against relaxing its vigilant and reserved posture toward Japan.
subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Secretary of State Regarding Foreign Minister Hirota's Address in the Diet
